items.content: Never judge a visual change by reasoning about the code. Run `npm run shots` and LOOK at docs/shots/<label>/, comparing against docs/shots/00-baseline/. Never ask the user what something looks like.
items.why: This project exists as a web port for exactly one reason: in the Godot original the agent could not see rendered output, so every art pass round-tripped through a human reviewer and the visual bar in sprite_style_guide.md was never met. The harness removes that bottleneck. Reintroducing the human-as-eyeball loop wastes the entire reason the port exists.

items.content: Skin shadows must use SHADOW_SKIN (rosy, hue 0.98); everything else uses SHADOW_COOL (blue-violet, 0.65). Hue interpolation always takes the short way around the circle. Never add a colour literal outside src/art/palette.ts, and give every migrated sprite a declared palette so bake() can snap to it.
items.why: Pushing skin's 27-degree hue toward blue-violet travels through yellow-green, so the shaded half of a face comes out olive - the single most damaging artefact on a character sprite. The style guide asks for red-brown on skin specifically for this reason. Separately, derived shades, cast shadows and the outline blend each mint a new colour per application: Maren measured 57 distinct colours on one 32x32 sprite before snapping, which is what makes a cast stop reading as one piece of art.
